quote: Please read the 7 questions below carefully and answer each one honestly: check YES or NO.
claim: The 2025 PAR-Q+ starts with 7 yes/no general health questions (heart condition or high blood pressure, chest pain, dizziness or loss of consciousness, other chronic condition, prescribed medication, bone/joint/soft-tissue problem, doctor-advised supervised activity); answering NO to all clears a person for physical activity.
population: adults (and minors with guardian signature) about to become more physically active
used_for: pre-participation screening at intake

quote: 2) Do you feel pain in your chest at rest, during your daily activities of living, OR when you do physical activity? 3) Do you lose balance because of dizziness OR have you lost consciousness in the last 12 months?
claim: Two of the 7 PAR-Q+ screening questions concern chest pain (at rest, in daily life or during activity) and dizziness with loss of balance or loss of consciousness in the last 12 months; dizziness linked to over-breathing during vigorous exercise is answered NO.
population: anyone completing the PAR-Q+
used_for: cardiac warning symptoms at intake

quote: If you answered YES to one or more of the questions above, COMPLETE PAGES 2 AND 3.
claim: Any YES on the 7 general questions does not by itself bar exercise: it triggers condition-specific follow-up questions (pages 2-3).
population: anyone completing the PAR-Q+
used_for: routing after a positive screen

quote: If you answered YES to one or more of the follow-up questions about your medical condition: You should seek further information before becoming more physically active or engaging in a fitness appraisal. You should complete the specially designed online screening and exercise recommendations program - the ePARmed-X+ at www.eparmedx.com and/or visit a qualified exercise professional
claim: A YES to any PAR-Q+ follow-up question means the person should get further information before becoming more active or doing a fitness test: complete the online ePARmed-X+ and/or see a qualified exercise professional.
population: people with a YES on a PAR-Q+ follow-up question
used_for: referral routing after screening
caveat: The form adds 'If in doubt after completing the questionnaire, consult your doctor prior to physical activity.'

quote: If you are over the age of 45 yr and NOT accustomed to regular vigorous to maximal effort exercise, consult a qualified exercise professional before engaging in this intensity of exercise.
claim: Even when cleared, people over 45 who are not used to regular vigorous-to-maximal exercise should consult a qualified exercise professional before training at that intensity.
population: adults over 45 years without recent vigorous training
used_for: intensity gating for older beginners

quote: Delay becoming more active if: You are currently experiencing a temporary illness, such as a cold or fever. It is best to wait until you feel better.
claim: The PAR-Q+ advises delaying an increase in activity during a temporary illness such as a cold or fever, during pregnancy (talk to a health professional or complete the ePARmed-X+), and when health changes.
population: anyone completing the PAR-Q+
used_for: when to delay starting or progressing
caveat: Return-to-training rules after illness belong to the MON cluster; pregnancy to POP.

quote: I acknowledge that this physical activity clearance is valid for a maximum of 12 months from the date it is completed and becomes invalid if my condition changes.
claim: A PAR-Q+ clearance is valid for at most 12 months and becomes invalid as soon as the person's condition changes, so screening must be repeated yearly and after any health change.
population: anyone completing the PAR-Q+
used_for: re-screening interval

quote: You are encouraged to start slowly and build up gradually - 20 to 60 minutes of low to moderate intensity exercise, 3-5 days per week including aerobic and muscle strengthening exercises.
claim: People cleared after the PAR-Q+ follow-up are advised to start slowly with 20-60 minutes of low-to-moderate intensity exercise on 3-5 days per week, including aerobic and muscle-strengthening work, building towards 150 minutes or more of moderate activity per week.
population: people cleared by the PAR-Q+
used_for: starting dose for newly cleared beginners

quote: The roundtable proposed a new evidence-informed model for exercise preparticipation health screening on the basis of three factors: 1) the individual's current level of physical activity, 2) presence of signs or symptoms and/or known cardiovascular, metabolic, or renal disease, and 3) desired exercise intensity
claim: ACSM pre-participation screening rests on three factors: current physical activity, signs or symptoms and/or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, and the desired exercise intensity; cardiovascular risk-factor profiling is no longer part of the screening decision.
population: adults starting or increasing exercise (ACSM model)
used_for: screening logic

quote: there is considerable evidence that exercise is safe for most people and has many associated health and fitness benefits; exercise-related cardiovascular events are often preceded by warning signs/symptoms; and the cardiovascular risks associated with exercise lessen as individuals become more physically active/fit
claim: Exercise is safe for most people; exercise-related cardiovascular events are often preceded by warning signs or symptoms, and cardiovascular risk falls as people become more active and fit, which is why symptom reporting matters more than risk-factor counting.
population: adults (ACSM roundtable evidence summary)
used_for: why to ask about symptoms every session

quote: Exercise Participation Performing planned, structured physical activity at least 30 min at moderate intensity on at least 3 d∙wk−1 for at least the last 3 months.
claim: In the ACSM algorithm (reproduced from Riebe 2015) a person counts as a regular exerciser only after planned, structured activity of at least 30 min at moderate intensity on at least 3 days per week for at least the last 3 months.
population: adults screened with the 2015 ACSM algorithm
used_for: classifying active vs inactive at intake

quote: Vigorous Intensity Exercise ≥60% HRR or VO2R, ≥6 METs, ≥14 RPE, an intensity that causes substantial increases in HR and breathing
claim: In the ACSM screening algorithm, vigorous intensity means at least 60% of heart-rate or VO2 reserve, at least 6 METs or RPE 14 or higher; moderate is 40 to under 60% HRR, 3 to under 6 METs, RPE 12-13.
population: adults screened with the 2015 ACSM algorithm
used_for: deciding when clearance before vigorous training applies

quote: Asymptomatic respondents with no history of the specified diseases are recommended to begin light to moderate intensity physical exercise without clearance, and gradually progress per ACSM guidelines Asymptomatic respondents with a positive history of the specified diseases are recommended to seek medical clearance before beginning exercise of any intensity Symptomatic respondents, regardless of history, are recommended to seek medical clearance before beginning exercise of any intensity
claim: For people not currently exercising: without symptoms or known cardiovascular, metabolic or renal disease, start light-to-moderate exercise without medical clearance and progress gradually; with known disease (even without symptoms) or with any symptoms, get medical clearance before exercise of any intensity.
population: inactive adults (ACSM 2015 algorithm)
used_for: medical clearance decision for beginners
caveat: Chronic disease management itself belongs to the POP cluster; here only the clearance trigger is used.

quote: Asymptomatic respondents with no history of the specified diseases are encouraged to continue moderate or vigorous intensity exercise without clearance, and gradually progress per ACSM guidelines Asymptomatic respondents with a positive history of the specified diseases are encouraged to continue light to moderate intensity exercise without clearance, but should have medical clearance before progressing to vigorous intensity exercise Symptomatic respondents, regardless of history, are recommended to seek medical clearance before continuing exercise of any intensity
claim: For people already exercising regularly: without symptoms or known disease, continue moderate or vigorous training and progress gradually; with known disease but no symptoms, continue light-to-moderate training but get medical clearance before progressing to vigorous; with any new symptoms, stop and get medical clearance before continuing at any intensity.
population: regularly active adults (ACSM 2015 algorithm)
used_for: medical clearance decision for trained athletes

quote: Signs and Symptoms At rest or during activity; includes pain, discomfort in the chest, neck, jaw, arms, or other areas that may result from ischemia; shortness of breath at rest or with mild exertion; dizziness or syncope; orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea; ankle edema; palpitations or tachycardia; intermittent claudication; known heart murmur; or unusual fatigue or shortness of breath with usual activities.
claim: Signs and symptoms that trigger medical clearance in the ACSM algorithm: chest, neck, jaw or arm pain or discomfort; shortness of breath at rest or on mild exertion; dizziness or fainting; breathlessness lying down or waking at night breathless; ankle swelling; palpitations or racing heart; calf pain on walking (claudication); known heart murmur; unusual fatigue or breathlessness with usual activities.
population: adults screened with the 2015 ACSM algorithm
used_for: symptom checklist the agent asks about

quote: vigorous physical activity, particularly when performed by unfit individuals, can acutely increase the risk of sudden cardiac death and acute myocardial infarction in susceptible people
claim: Vigorous activity, especially in unfit people, transiently raises the risk of sudden cardiac death and heart attack in susceptible individuals, while regular activity lowers coronary risk overall; this is why unaccustomed people should build up gradually.
population: adults, especially unfit or with underlying heart disease (AHA statement)
used_for: justifying gradual progression and symptom vigilance

quote: Immediate action required: Call 999 if: you have chest pain that feels tight or like squeezing on your chest you have chest pain that's spreading to your arms, neck or jaw you're having severe difficulty breathing
claim: Call the emergency number immediately (999 in the UK; 112 in the EU) for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, chest pain spreading to the arms, neck or jaw, severe difficulty breathing, pale/blue/grey lips or skin, or if someone has passed out and is not responding normally.
population: general public (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: chest pain during exercise: emergency trigger
caveat: 999 is the UK number; for EU users give 112 (EC-112).

quote: Do not drive yourself to A&E.
claim: A person with possible heart-attack symptoms should not drive themselves to hospital.
population: general public (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: chest pain scenario: what not to do

quote: Sit and rest on the floor in a comfortable position, with your knees bent and your back supported.
claim: While waiting for help, the person should stop all activity and sit and rest, supported; if they stop responding and stop breathing, bystanders should start CPR.
population: general public (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: chest pain scenario: immediate actions
caveat: The page also suggests aspirin and GTN; medication advice is outside the coach's scope, so the agent leaves that to the emergency dispatcher.

quote: Urgent advice: Call NHS 111 if: you're suddenly more short of breath than usual you have chest pain and you feel sick or are being sick you have chest pain and you feel like your heart is racing, going too slowly, skipping a beat or have a fluttering feeling in your chest
claim: Sudden unusual breathlessness, or chest pain with nausea/vomiting or with a racing, slow, skipping or fluttering heartbeat, needs same-day urgent medical advice even when it does not meet the immediate-emergency criteria.
population: general public (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: palpitations and breathlessness: urgent referral
caveat: 111 is the UK non-emergency medical line; outside the UK the agent advises contacting a doctor or emergency services urgently.

quote: 112 is the European emergency phone number, available everywhere in the EU, free of charge. How does it work? You can call 112 from fixed and mobile phones to contact any emergency service: an ambulance, the fire brigade or the police.
claim: 112 is the European emergency number: free, available everywhere in the EU from fixed and mobile phones, and connects to ambulance, fire brigade or police; it is also used in some non-EU countries and works worldwide on GSM mobile networks.
population: anyone in the EU
used_for: emergency number given in every emergency instruction

quote: you cannot move your knee or put any weight on it your knee is badly swollen or has changed shape your knee locks, gives way or painfully clicks – painless clicking is normal
claim: Knee pain needs same-day urgent medical advice (not exercise modification) if the person cannot move the knee or put any weight on it, the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or it locks, gives way or clicks painfully; painless clicking is normal.
population: general public with knee pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: knee pain during squats: urgent referral triggers
caveat: The NHS routes these to its 111 urgent advice line; outside the UK use the local urgent-care or out-of-hours service, and 112 if the person cannot be moved or is seriously hurt.

quote: you have a very high temperature (or feel hot, cold or shivery) and have redness or heat around your knee – this can be a sign of infection
claim: Knee pain with a very high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery, together with redness or heat around the knee, can signal a joint infection and needs urgent medical advice.
population: general public with knee pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: systemic symptoms with joint pain: urgent referral

quote: Non-urgent advice: See a GP if: knee pain does not improve within a few weeks
claim: Knee pain without urgent signs often settles with self-care; it warrants a GP (or physiotherapy) appointment if it does not improve within a few weeks.
population: general public with knee pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: knee pain: refer-soon trigger
caveat: 'A few weeks' is not defined more precisely in the source.

quote: This information might give you an idea of what the cause might be. But do not self-diagnose – see a GP if you're worried.
claim: Knee pain has many possible causes (sprain, tendon problems, ligament or meniscus tear, osteoarthritis, bursitis, infection and others); the NHS explicitly advises against self-diagnosis and to see a GP if worried, so a coach should not name a cause either.
population: general public with knee pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: no diagnosis by the coach

quote: Unable to weight bear immediately after the injury or for four steps in the emergency department
claim: Under the Ottawa ankle rules, X-ray is warranted after an acute ankle injury if the person was unable to bear weight immediately after the injury or cannot take four steps, or has bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either ankle bone (malleolus).
population: adults with acute ankle injury assessed in emergency departments
used_for: acute joint injury: inability to bear weight means referral
caveat: Clinical decision rule applied by clinicians; the coach uses only the weight-bearing part as a referral trigger and does not palpate or diagnose.

quote: 15 were included, involving 8560 patients from 13 countries. Sensitivity, specificity, negative likelihood ratio, positive likelihood ratio and diagnostic odds ratio were 0.91 (95% CI, 0.89 to 0.92), 0.25 (95% CI, 0.24 to 0.26)
claim: The Ottawa ankle rule is highly sensitive (pooled sensitivity 0.91) but not specific (0.25) for ankle fracture, so a positive result means 'get it checked', not 'it is broken'.
population: adults with acute ankle injury (15 studies, 8560 patients, 13 countries)
used_for: acute ankle injury referral threshold

quote: Statement 2. The core criterion required to define PFP is pain around or behind the patella, which is aggravated by at least one activity that loads the patellofemoral joint during weight bearing on a flexed knee (eg, squatting, stair ambulation, jogging/running, hopping/jumping).
claim: Pain around or behind the kneecap that is aggravated by loaded flexed-knee activities such as squatting, stairs, running or jumping is the core feature of patellofemoral pain, a common condition in active people; the label itself is a clinical diagnosis.
population: active adolescents and adults (international research consensus)
used_for: knee pain during squats: context only, no labelling by the coach

quote: Clinical examination is the cornerstone to diagnose PFP,16 17 but there is no definitive clinical test to diagnose PFP.
claim: Patellofemoral pain is diagnosed by clinical examination and there is no definitive test; a person with a history of kneecap dislocation or a feeling of the kneecap slipping belongs to a distinct subgroup needing different management.
population: active adolescents and adults (international research consensus)
used_for: why the coach refers rather than diagnoses knee pain

quote: Briefly, pain levels should not exceed a 5/10 on the numeric pain rating scale (NPRS) during or immediately after activity. Additionally, pain ratings should return to pre-activity levels by the following morning.
claim: Pain-monitoring model: during and immediately after activity, pain should not exceed 5/10 on a numeric pain rating scale, and it should return to the pre-activity level by the next morning; if not, the load is reduced.
population: people with tendinopathy or patellofemoral pain in rehabilitation (model described by Thomee, adapted by Silbernagel)
used_for: acceptable pain during exercise (continue-with-modification criterion)
caveat: Rule of thumb from rehabilitation of diagnosed tendinopathy and patellofemoral pain; supported by one RCT (38 patients) and a feasibility pilot, not validated for undiagnosed pain. Use only when no red flags are present.

quote: Thirty-eight patients with Achilles tendinopathy were randomly allocated to 2 different treatment groups. The exercise training group (n = 19) was allowed, with the use of a pain-monitoring model, to continue Achilles tendon-loading activity, such as running and jumping, whereas the active rest group (n = 19) had to stop such activities during the first 6 weeks.
claim: In an RCT of Achilles tendinopathy (19 patients per group), continuing running and jumping guided by the pain-monitoring model gave the same improvement as 6 weeks of active rest, with no negative effects.
population: adults with Achilles tendinopathy (RCT, n = 38)
used_for: evidence that pain-monitored continuation is not harmful
caveat: Small single trial in one diagnosed condition.

quote: There was short- term significant difference in pain, with moderate quality evidence for a small effect size of -0.27 (-0.54 to -0.05) in favour of painful exercises. For pain in the medium and long term, and function and disability in the short, medium and long term, there was no significant difference.
claim: In chronic musculoskeletal pain, exercises where some pain is allowed gave a small short-term benefit for pain (effect size -0.27) over pain-free exercises and were no worse in the medium and long term; some pain during exercise need not be a barrier.
population: adults with chronic (over 3 months) musculoskeletal pain (7 RCTs, 385 participants)
used_for: acceptable pain during exercise
caveat: Applies to chronic pain already assessed by a clinician, not to new or acute pain.

quote: Immediate action required: Call 999 or go to A&E if: You have back pain and: pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs a loss of feeling around your genitals or anus changes in your bladder or bowels, such as difficulty peeing, or peeing or pooing yourself
claim: Back pain with pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs, loss of feeling around the genitals or anus, or new bladder or bowel changes needs an emergency call (999 in the UK; 112 in the EU) or emergency department; so does back pain with chest pain or after a serious accident.
population: general public with back pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: spinal emergency red flags (possible cauda equina syndrome)
caveat: 999 is the UK number; give 112 in the EU (EC-112).

quote: Urgent advice: Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from 111 if: You have back pain and: you feel hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell it's severe pain that starts suddenly, or it's getting worse quickly
claim: Back pain with feeling hot, cold, shivery or generally unwell, or severe pain that starts suddenly or worsens quickly, needs an urgent same-day medical appointment.
population: general public with back pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: spinal red flags: urgent referral (systemic symptoms)

quote: you've lost weight without trying to there's a lump or swelling in your back, or your back has changed shape it does not improve after resting or is worse at night
claim: Back pain should be seen by a GP if there is unexplained weight loss, a lump or change of shape in the back, pain that does not ease with rest or is worse at night, or pain that has not improved after a few weeks of self-care.
population: general public with back pain (NHS England patient guidance)
used_for: night pain and unexplained weight loss: refer-soon triggers

quote: All included papers recommended urgent MRI with the presence of red flag findings. Red flags included in all papers were perianal/perineal/saddle sensory disturbance and bladder or bowel dysfunction of varying specifications. 8/9 papers included radicular/sciatic pain, 5/9 included new motor weakness
claim: All 9 international cauda equina pathways list saddle-area numbness and bladder or bowel dysfunction as red flags requiring urgent imaging; most also list sciatic pain (8/9) and new leg weakness (5/9).
population: adults with suspected cauda equina syndrome (systematic review of 9 guidelines)
used_for: spinal emergency red flags

quote: Many red flags in current guidelines provide virtually no change in probability of fracture or malignancy or have untested diagnostic accuracy.
claim: Most single low-back-pain red flags change the probability of fracture or cancer very little; the more informative ones are a history of cancer, prolonged corticosteroid use, severe trauma, and the presence of several red flags together.
population: patients with low back pain in primary, secondary or tertiary care (14 studies, 53 red flags)
used_for: why red flags trigger referral rather than a conclusion
caveat: Applies to clinicians' diagnostic reasoning; for the coach the practical rule is simply to refer when any listed sign is present.

quote: While rare, serious spinal pathology can have devastating and life-changing or life-limiting consequences, and must be identified early and managed appropriately. ... Currently, there is an absence of high-quality evidence for the diagnostic accuracy of most red flags.
claim: Serious spinal pathology is rare but must be identified early; because most red flags lack high-quality diagnostic evidence, the international IFOMPT framework uses them inside clinical reasoning rather than as stand-alone tests.
population: people with spinal pain assessed by clinicians (international framework)
used_for: spinal red flags: framing

quote: The 2 main diagnostic criteria for EHS are CNS dysfunction and a core body temperature greater than 40.5°C (105°F).16,19,52 However, if a suspected EHS victim exhibits CNS dysfunction even though the rectal temperature is slightly lower (ie, 40°C [104°F]), it is prudent to assume the patient is suffering from EHS
claim: Exertional heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction plus core temperature above 40.5 C; anyone exercising in the heat who becomes confused or behaves abnormally should be treated as heat stroke even if the temperature is slightly lower (40 C) or unknown.
population: athletes and physically active people exercising in heat (NATA position statement)
used_for: exertional heat stroke recognition

quote: Common clinical presentations of EHS may include: collapse, confusion, aggressiveness, hysteria, delirium, altered consciousness, irrational behaviour, irritability, seizures, dehydration, hyperthermia, diarrhoea, vomiting, dizziness, fatigue and weakness. Since a sudden collapse can also be the result of cardiac arrest
claim: Signs of exertional heat stroke include collapse, confusion, aggressiveness, irrational behaviour, altered consciousness, seizures, vomiting, dizziness and weakness; because a sudden collapse can also be cardiac arrest, responsiveness and breathing are checked first.
population: athletes at sports competitions in heat (IOC expert working group)
used_for: exertional heat stroke recognition

quote: If EHS is suspected, CWI (or another rapid cooling mechanism if CWI is not available) should be initiated immediately.
claim: When exertional heat stroke is suspected, start whole-body cold-water immersion immediately (or the fastest cooling available, such as cold-water dousing with fans or ice-water towels) and do not waste time on an invalid temperature method.
population: athletes and physically active people (NATA position statement)
used_for: exertional heat stroke: first action

quote: Timely (less than 30 minutes from the time of collapse) CWI therapy was associated with a 0% fatality rate in more than 2000 EHS patients in athletics and military settings.
claim: Cold-water immersion started within 30 minutes of collapse was associated with 0% deaths in more than 2000 exertional heat stroke patients; other cooling methods work more slowly.
population: athletes and military personnel with exertional heat stroke
used_for: exertional heat stroke: why cooling comes first

quote: For any EHS patient, the goal is to lower core body temperature to less than 38.9°C (102°F) within 30 minutes of collapse.
claim: The cooling goal in exertional heat stroke is a core temperature below 38.9 C within 30 minutes of collapse.
population: athletes and physically active people (NATA position statement)
used_for: exertional heat stroke cooling target

quote: If rectal temperature cannot be measured and cold-water immersion is indicated, cool for 10–15 min and then transport to a medical facility.
claim: If core temperature cannot be measured, cool by cold-water immersion for 10-15 minutes and then transport to a medical facility by emergency services.
population: athletes and physically active people (NATA position statement)
used_for: exertional heat stroke cooling without a rectal thermometer

quote: No other field-expedient methods of obtaining core body temperature (eg, oral, axillary, tympanic, forehead sticker, temporal) are valid or reliable after intense exercise in the heat
claim: Oral, armpit, ear, forehead and temporal thermometers are not valid after intense exercise in the heat; only rectal temperature is, so a normal reading from these devices must not rule out heat stroke.
population: athletes exercising in heat (NATA position statement)
used_for: do not trust field thermometers

quote: Identifying the athlete with suspected exertional heat stroke early in the course, stopping activity (body heat generation), and providing rapid total body cooling are essential for survival, and like any critical life-threatening situation (cardiac arrest, brain stroke, sepsis), time is tissue.
claim: Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency: recognise it early, stop activity and provide rapid whole-body cooling; outcomes depend on how long severe hyperthermia lasts.
population: athletes and physically active people (ACSM expert consensus)
used_for: exertional heat stroke: emergency framing

quote: In all cases of EHS, after the patient has completed a 7- to 21-day rest period, demonstrated normal blood-work results, and obtained physician clearance
claim: After exertional heat stroke, training resumes only after a 7- to 21-day rest, normal blood tests and physician clearance, then progresses gradually from low to high intensity in a temperate environment.
population: athletes recovering from exertional heat stroke (NATA position statement)
used_for: return to training after heat stroke: physician-led

quote: Exercise-associated hyponatremia (EAH) is defined by a serum or plasma sodium concentration below the normal reference range of 135 mmol·L-1 that occurs during or up to 24 h after prolonged physical activity.
claim: Exercise-associated hyponatremia is a blood sodium below 135 mmol/L during or up to 24 h after prolonged activity; its signs overlap with heat exhaustion and heat stroke, so it can only be confirmed by a blood test.
population: people doing prolonged endurance activity, including wilderness and organised events (WMS guideline)
used_for: hyponatremia recognition

quote: Sixth, the most common mild EAH complaints were nausea, weakness or lethargy, dizziness, headache, and extremity swelling. Seventh, the most common SAS of moderate-to-severe EAH (ie, suggesting hyponatremic encephalopathy) included altered mental status, vomiting, seizure, agitation/restlessness, collapse, and loss of consciousness.
claim: Mild exercise-associated hyponatremia most often shows as nausea, weakness, dizziness, headache and swollen hands or feet; moderate-to-severe cases show confusion, vomiting, seizures, agitation, collapse or loss of consciousness, which is an emergency.
population: endurance participants (220 EAH cases from 56 field studies, events of 5-29.5 h)
used_for: hyponatremia warning signs

quote: This complex, dynamic clinical condition may result from excessive fluid intake (ie, exceeding the volume of sweat secreted), a large sodium loss in sweat, inappropriate mobilization of internal sodium stores, and/or inappropriately elevated blood arginine vasopressin concentration (ie, renal water retention which lowers [Na+]).
claim: Exercise-associated hyponatremia results mainly from too much body water relative to sodium, for example drinking more than is sweated out; mild cases can progress rapidly to life-threatening brain swelling.
population: endurance participants (narrative review of field cases)
used_for: hyponatremia: cause and urgency
caveat: Fluid and sodium targets belong to cluster NUT.

quote: Pain and tenderness to palpation usually are severe or out of proportion to what one would normally expect from the activity, ... Muscle swelling, ... Significant limitation in active and passive range of motion, ... Weakness, especially when the hip and shoulder girdle muscles are involved, ... Presence of cola-colored urine, and/or ... Persistent, non-improving or worsening pain and soreness for more than 5–7 days after the causal activity.
claim: Features that distinguish exertional rhabdomyolysis from normal muscle soreness: pain out of proportion to the session, muscle swelling, marked loss of range of motion, weakness (especially hip and shoulder muscles), cola-coloured urine, or soreness that worsens or persists beyond 5-7 days.
population: military trainees and athletes after strenuous or unaccustomed exercise (military clinical practice guideline)
used_for: rhabdomyolysis warning signs

quote: BLUF: While an onset of dark urine within 24 hours following strenuous exercise is highly suggestive of ER
claim: Dark urine appearing within 24 hours after strenuous exercise is highly suggestive of exertional rhabdomyolysis and needs same-day medical assessment.
population: military trainees and athletes (military clinical practice guideline)
used_for: rhabdomyolysis: urgent referral trigger

quote: High-intensity, repetitive, or prolonged unaccustomed exercise unmatched to fitness level; excessively motivated individual; inexperienced trainers and/or leaders; medications or dietary supplement use (especially stimulants); hot and humid climate
claim: Exertional rhabdomyolysis is promoted by high-intensity, repetitive or prolonged unaccustomed exercise unmatched to fitness, an over-motivated athlete, inexperienced trainers, stimulant supplements or medications, and hot humid conditions.
population: military trainees and athletes (military clinical practice guideline)
used_for: rhabdomyolysis prevention in programming

quote: A diagnosis of exertional rhabdomyolysis (ER) is made when there are severe muscle symptoms (pain, stiffness, and/or weakness) AND laboratory evidence of myonecrosis with a creatine kinase (CK) level ≥5,000 IU/L
claim: Exertional rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed only with a blood test (creatine kinase at least 5,000 IU/L) plus severe muscle symptoms after exercise, so suspicion means referral, not coach judgement.
population: military trainees and athletes (military clinical practice guideline)
used_for: rhabdomyolysis: diagnosis is medical

quote: Neck pain or tenderness ... Severe or increasing headache ... Deteriorating conscious state ... Double vision ... Seizure or convulsion ... Vomiting ... Weakness or tingling/ burning in arms of legs ... Loss of consciousness ... Increasingly restless, agitated or combative
claim: Concussion red flags that require an ambulance after a head impact: neck pain or tenderness, severe or increasing headache, deteriorating consciousness, double vision, seizure, vomiting, weakness or tingling/burning in arms or legs, loss of consciousness, or increasing restlessness, agitation or combativeness.
population: children, adolescents and adults after a head impact in sport (CRT6)
used_for: concussion red flags (falls in climbing, cycling crashes)

quote: ANY ATHLETE WITH A SUSPECTED CONCUSSION SHOULD BE IMMEDIATELY REMOVED FROM TRAINING/COMPETITION OR ACTIVITY AND SHOULD NOT RETURN TO ACTIVITY UNTIL ASSESSED MEDICALLY, EVEN IF THE SYMPTOMS RESOLVE
claim: Any athlete with suspected concussion must stop the activity immediately and not return until assessed medically, even if symptoms resolve.
population: children, adolescents and adults after a head impact in sport (CRT6)
used_for: concussion: remove and refer

quote: Not be left alone initially (at least for the first 1-2 hours). · Not use recreational/prescription drugs. · Not be sent home by themselves. They need to be with a responsible adult. · Not drive a motor vehicle until cleared to do so by a health professional.
claim: A person with suspected concussion should not be left alone for at least the first 1-2 hours, should not drink alcohol or use drugs, should not go home alone and should not drive until cleared by a health professional.
population: children, adolescents and adults after a head impact in sport (CRT6)
used_for: concussion: immediate aftercare

quote: Do not attempt to move the skier/ snowboarder (other than required for airway support) unless trained to do so. ... Assessment for a spinal cord injury is critical. ... Do not remove a helmet or any other equipment unless trained to do so safely.
claim: After a fall or crash with head impact, do not move the person (except to keep the airway open) or remove the helmet unless trained, because a spinal cord injury must be assessed first.
population: athletes after a fall or crash (CRT6, FIS version)
used_for: falls in climbing, cycling crashes: first aid

quote: This functional overreaching will eventually lead to an improvement in performance after recovery. When athletes do not sufficiently respect the balance between training and recovery, nonfunctional overreaching (NFOR) can occur. The distinction between NFOR and overtraining syndrome (OTS) is very difficult and will depend on the clinical outcome and exclusion diagnosis.
claim: Functional overreaching is a short-term performance dip that turns into improvement after recovery; when training and recovery stay out of balance, non-functional overreaching can follow, and telling it apart from overtraining syndrome depends on the clinical course and exclusion of other diagnoses.
population: athletes (joint ECSS/ACSM consensus)
used_for: overreaching versus overtraining

quote: One approach to understanding the etiology of OTS involves the exclusion of organic diseases or infections and factors such as dietary caloric restriction (negative energy balance) and insufficient carbohydrate and/or protein intake, iron deficiency, magnesium deficiency, allergies, and others
claim: Diagnosing overtraining syndrome requires excluding disease, infection, energy deficit, low carbohydrate or protein intake, iron or magnesium deficiency, allergies and other causes; no single marker (hormones, performance or psychological tests, blood markers) is accepted for diagnosis.
population: athletes (joint ECSS/ACSM consensus)
used_for: unexplained underperformance: refer to a physician
caveat: Consensus is more than 10 years old (2013); no newer joint statement found.

quote: to minimise the risk of non-functional overreaching (fatigue lasting weeks to months),
claim: Non-functional overreaching means fatigue lasting weeks to months, as opposed to the days of normal acute fatigue after hard training.
population: athletes (IOC consensus on load and injury)
used_for: when fatigue becomes a referral question
caveat: The 'days' contrast is the usual reading of the fatigue continuum; the source states only the weeks-to-months duration.

quote: A prior history of DE behaviours or an ED might perpetuate a continued under-­fuelling of energy1 and must therefore be considered an important risk factor for developing REDs. DE behaviours and EDs may be exacerbated by social media influence, societal pressures, the athlete’s training/coaching entourage, a belief that a specific physique/weight/appearance will improve performance
claim: Disordered eating, eating disorders and REDs are common in some athlete groups; a past eating disorder is an important risk factor, and the coaching environment and beliefs that a certain weight or physique improves performance can make them worse.
population: athletes of all sexes and levels (IOC consensus 2023)
used_for: REDs and disordered eating: coach awareness

quote: and coach in making informed ‘health first–performance second’ decisions relating to body composition manipulation.26 132 This should include prescreening to assess body image concerns and problematic eating behaviours
claim: Body-composition changes should be decided 'health first, performance second' by trained health staff, with prior screening for body-image concerns and problematic eating; coaches are named as a common source of pressure on weight.
population: athletes (IOC consensus 2023)
used_for: weight and body composition goals: coach boundaries

quote: Step 1: implementation of population-­specific validated REDs Screening Questionnaire(s) and/or clinical interviews, which are less sensitive and objective but inexpensive and easy to implement for the initial identification of athletes at risk; Step 2: implementation of the IOC REDs CAT2 Severity/ Risk Assessment
claim: The IOC REDs assessment runs in three steps: screening questionnaires or interviews to flag athletes at risk (cheap but less sensitive), a severity and risk assessment with a traffic-light outcome, and diagnosis by an expert physician with a multidisciplinary team.
population: athletes (IOC consensus 2023)
used_for: REDs screening: where the coach fits

quote: Disclaimer: these guidelines are not to be used in isolation and are not to be solely used for diagnosis. Furthermore, these guidelines are less reliable when it is impossible to assess all indicators in table 4. These guidelines are not a substitute for professional clinical diagnosis, advice and/or treatment from a team of REDs health and performance experts led by a physician.
claim: REDs screening and risk tools must not be used alone or as a diagnosis; they are no substitute for diagnosis and treatment by a physician-led team.
population: athletes (IOC consensus 2023)
used_for: limits of REDs screening tools

quote: Secondary amenorrhoea (females: absence of 3–11 consecutive menstrual cycles) caused by FHA
claim: Missing 3-11 consecutive menstrual periods (secondary amenorrhoea from low energy availability) is a primary REDs indicator.
population: female athletes (IOC REDs CAT2)
used_for: REDs warning sign the athlete may report

quote: Oligomenorrhoea caused by FHA (>35 days between periods for a maximum of 8 periods/year)
claim: Cycles longer than 35 days (at most 8 periods a year) are a secondary REDs indicator.
population: female athletes (IOC REDs CAT2)
used_for: REDs warning sign the athlete may report

quote: History of ≥1 high-­risk (femoral neck, sacrum, pelvis) or ≥2 low-­risk BSI (all other BSI locations) within the previous 2 years
claim: A history of at least 1 high-risk bone stress injury (femoral neck, sacrum, pelvis) or at least 2 other bone stress injuries in the previous 2 years is a primary REDs indicator.
population: athletes (IOC REDs CAT2)
used_for: REDs warning sign from injury history

quote: An elevated score for the EDE-­Q global (>2.30 in females; >1.68 in males) and/or clinically diagnosed DSM-­5-­TR-­defined Eating Disorder
claim: An elevated Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire global score (above 2.30 in females, above 1.68 in males) or a diagnosed eating disorder is a primary REDs indicator.
population: athletes (IOC REDs CAT2)
used_for: disordered eating screening tool and cut-offs
caveat: Questionnaire scoring and interpretation belong to qualified health professionals; the coach does not administer or interpret it.

quote: A negative deviation of a paediatric or adolescent athlete’s previous growth trajectory (height and/or weight)
claim: In children and adolescents, falling off their previous growth curve for height or weight is a primary REDs indicator.
population: paediatric and adolescent athletes (IOC REDs CAT2)
used_for: REDs warning sign in young athletes

quote: The consensus (IOC 2023) is that energy availability, which is at the core of REDs syndrome, is impossible to measure accurately enough in the field, and therefore, the only way to diagnose an athlete with REDs appears to be by studying symptom presentation and risk factors. However, the symptoms are rather generic, and the causes likely multifactorial.
claim: Critics argue that because energy availability cannot be measured accurately in the field and REDs symptoms are generic and multifactorial, labelling an athlete with 'REDs syndrome' from symptoms risks missing other causes.
population: athletes (critical narrative review)
used_for: REDs: why the coach must not label

quote: AUSactive Registered Exercise Professionals are qualified to plan and deliver exercise for low and moderate risk clientele based on the industry endorsed Pre-exercise Screening systems 1 2. AUSactive Registered Exercise Professionals may work with higher risk clientele (whose conditions are stabilised and managed) after making a written referral to and receiving documented guidance on the exercise program from the clients’ treating medical and/or allied health practitioner.
claim: Registered exercise professionals plan exercise independently only for low- and moderate-risk clients identified by pre-exercise screening; higher-risk clients with stable, managed conditions are trained only after written referral to and documented guidance from their treating health practitioner.
population: registered exercise professionals in Australia (personal trainers, gym and group instructors)
used_for: scope of practice: who the coach can program for

quote: A. Provision of nutritional advice outside of basic healthy eating information and nationally endorsed nutritional standards and guidelines B. Therapeutic treatment or independent rehabilitative exercise prescription C. Independent exercise prescription for high risk clients D. Diagnostic tests or procedures
claim: The scope of a registered exercise professional excludes nutrition advice beyond basic healthy-eating guidelines, therapeutic treatment or independent rehabilitation, independent programming for high-risk clients, diagnostic tests or procedures, and psychological counselling.
population: registered exercise professionals in Australia
used_for: scope of practice: what the coach must not do
caveat: One national register's statement; no equivalent EU-wide statement was found. Medication is not mentioned explicitly.

quote: B. Referring to medical or allied health professionals for guidance. Utilising best practice referral/ feedback processes to optimise client health outcomes
claim: Referring clients to medical or allied health professionals, with a referral and feedback loop, is part of a personal trainer's scope, alongside pre-exercise screening, risk management and first aid.
population: registered exercise professionals in Australia

quote: PED use has been linked to an increased risk of death and a wide variety of cardiovascular, psychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, neurologic, infectious, hepatic, renal, and musculoskeletal disorders.
claim: Performance-enhancing drug use, mostly by non-athlete weightlifters taking supraphysiological doses and combinations, is linked to higher risk of death and to cardiovascular, psychiatric, metabolic, endocrine, neurological, infectious, liver, kidney and musculoskeletal disorders.
population: users of performance-enhancing drugs, mostly recreational weightlifters (Endocrine Society statement)
used_for: steroid question: health risks
caveat: Statement is more than 10 years old (2014).

quote: the analysis yielded an estimate that 32.5% (95% conference interval, 25.4%–39.7%) of AAS users develop AAS dependence.
claim: About one in three anabolic-androgenic steroid users (estimate 32.5%) develop dependence.
population: anabolic-androgenic steroid users (pooled estimate from 10 studies, cited in Endocrine Society statement)
used_for: steroid question: dependence risk

quote: users will gradually develop suppressed testosterone levels and may become hypogonadal upon discontinuation of AAS use.
claim: Anabolic steroids suppress the body's own testosterone production; after stopping, many users have profound hypogonadism for weeks or months, with fatigue, low libido and depression that push them to restart.
population: male anabolic-androgenic steroid users (Endocrine Society statement)

quote: They have also been associated with life-threatening reactions such as: Kidney damage Heart attack Stroke Pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs) Deep vein thrombosis
claim: The FDA warns that anabolic steroids and steroid-like substances, including those hidden in products sold as dietary supplements, are associated with serious liver injury and with life-threatening kidney damage, heart attack, stroke and blood clots, as well as acne, hair loss, mood changes, aggression, depression, sexual dysfunction and testicular shrinkage.
population: consumers of bodybuilding products (US regulator warning)
used_for: steroid question: health risks

quote: the FDA recommends you immediately consult your health care professional because of the potentially serious health risks associated with using them and because of dangerous withdrawal problems that can arise from quickly ceasing the use of such products.
claim: Anyone already taking products that contain steroids or steroid-like substances should consult a health professional promptly, partly because stopping abruptly can cause dangerous withdrawal problems.
population: consumers of bodybuilding products (US regulator warning)

quote: To date, SARMs have no Food and Drug Administration approved use, and recent case reports associate the use of SARMs with deleterious effects such as drug-induced liver injury, myocarditis, and tendon rupture.
claim: SARMs have no FDA-approved use; case reports link them to drug-induced liver injury, myocarditis and tendon rupture, and products bought online are often contaminated and taken at doses above those studied.
population: athletes and recreational users (systematic review of 72 articles, mostly preclinical and case reports)
used_for: SARMs question: health risks and legal status
caveat: Evidence is mostly case reports and preclinical data; the review rates itself level 4.

quote: S1 ANABOLIC AGENTS PROHIBITED AT ALL TIMES (IN- AND OUT-OF-COMPETITION) All prohibited substances in this class are non-Specified Substances.
claim: Anabolic agents (WADA class S1, including anabolic-androgenic steroids) are prohibited at all times, in and out of competition, and are non-Specified Substances.

quote: S1.2. OTHER ANABOLIC AGENTS Including, but not limited to: Clenbuterol, osilodrostat, ractopamine, selective androgen receptor modulators [SARMs, e.g. andarine, enobosarm (ostarine), LGD-4033 (ligandrol), RAD140, S-23 and YK-11]
claim: SARMs such as ostarine (enobosarm), LGD-4033 (ligandrol), RAD140, S-23 and YK-11 are listed under S1.2 (other anabolic agents) and are prohibited at all times.

quote: ‘data concerning health’ means personal data related to the physical or mental health of a natural person, including the provision of health care services, which reveal information about his or her health status;
claim: GDPR Art. 4(15): 'data concerning health' is any personal data about a person's physical or mental health that reveals their health status (for an athlete, for example injuries, illness, symptoms, menstrual data, medical clearance).
population: anyone processing personal data in the EU (law)
used_for: athlete data privacy: what counts as health data
caveat: Legal text, not scientific evidence. The examples are the agent's reading, not text of the law.

quote: adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (‘data minimisation’);
claim: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c), data minimisation: personal data must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purpose.
population: anyone processing personal data in the EU (law)
used_for: athlete data sharing: minimisation

quote: data concerning health or data concerning a natural person's sex life or sexual orientation shall be prohibited. 2. Paragraph 1 shall not apply if one of the following applies: | (a) | the data subject has given explicit consent to the processing of those personal data for one or more specified purposes
claim: GDPR Art. 9(1)-(2)(a): processing health data is prohibited unless an exception applies, the first being the person's explicit consent for one or more specified purposes.
population: anyone processing personal data in the EU (law)
used_for: athlete health data: explicit consent
caveat: Art. 9(2) lists other exceptions; which legal basis applies to a given coaching business is a legal question outside the agent's scope.

quote: The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility.
claim: GDPR Art. 25(2), data protection by default: by default only the data necessary for each specific purpose are processed, which limits how much is collected, how far it is processed, how long it is kept and who can access it.
population: anyone processing personal data in the EU (law)
used_for: athlete data sharing: privacy by default

quote: 3. The data subject shall have the right to withdraw his or her consent at any time.
claim: GDPR Art. 7(3): a person can withdraw consent at any time, and withdrawing must be as easy as giving it.
population: anyone processing personal data in the EU (law)
used_for: athlete data: consent can be withdrawn

quote: Of 11 identified studies, 6 involving 4249 adult patients were considered appropriate for pooled analysis. The pooled negative likelihood ratio was 0.05 (95% CI, 0.02 to 0.23), the pooled sensitivity was 98.5% (CI, 93.2% to 100%), and the pooled specificity was 48.6% (CI, 43.4% to 51.0%).
claim: In a systematic review of the Ottawa knee rule after acute knee injury (6 studies pooled, 4249 adults), pooled sensitivity for fracture was 98.5% and specificity 48.6%: a negative result excludes a fracture, but about half of the patients with a positive result have no fracture.
population: adults with acute knee injury assessed in clinical settings (6 pooled studies, 4249 patients)
used_for: acute knee injury: why inability to bear weight means referral for assessment
caveat: The rule is applied by clinicians and the abstract does not list its items. The coach never applies the rule; inability to bear weight is only a referral trigger.

quote: Eight studies, including 7385 patients, were enrolled and pooled using the random effects model. Sensitivity, specificity, negative likelihood ratio, positive likelihood ratio and diagnostic odds ratio were 0.99 (95% CI, 0.97 to 1.00), 0.49 (95% CI, 0.47 to 0.51)
claim: A 2020 meta-analysis of the Ottawa knee rule in adults with acute knee injury (8 studies, 7385 patients) found pooled sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.49 for knee fracture: very good at ruling a fracture out, poor at confirming one, so a positive rule means 'get it imaged', not 'it is broken'.
population: adults with acute knee injury assessed by emergency physicians (8 studies, 7385 patients)
used_for: acute knee injury referral threshold, parallel to the Ottawa ankle rule (SAF-26, SAF-27)
caveat: Evidence for a clinician-applied decision rule in emergency departments. The coach does not apply it or palpate the knee; it only supports sending a person who cannot bear weight after a knee injury to medical assessment.

quote: While traditionally viewed as self-limiting, increasing research data suggest that patellofemoral pain is often recalcitrant and can persist for many years
claim: Patellofemoral pain, the common squat- and stair-related knee pain, is often stubborn and can persist for many years, so waiting for it to settle on its own is not a safe default and persistent pain should be referred.
population: physically active and sedentary people with patellofemoral pain (international research consensus)
used_for: knee pain during squats: do not assume it will self-resolve; refer if it persists
caveat: Exercise prescription for patellofemoral pain belongs to STR.
